notes.short: Like a good soldier of Christ Jesus
notes.about: Paul calls Timothy to share in suffering like a good soldier of Christ Jesus, and draws out the picture: a soldier on duty keeps clear of civilian affairs, to please the one who enlisted him. So Christ's servant is to bear hardship and keep himself free for his Master's service.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: like a good soldier of Christ Jesus
figure.means: Christ's servant, who bears hardship and keeps free of the business of this life to please his Lord, as a soldier pleases his commander

notes.evidence: Clarke says Paul considers a minister under the notion of a soldier, for the hardships he must bear. Barnes says Paul names one way the minister resembles the soldier, then another: neither is tied up in this life's affairs. Spence (Ellicott) calls verse 3 a simile and verse 4 its first picture; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), an illustration for Timothy to apply, its truths put in figures.
notes.limit: Most of the writers apply the picture chiefly to ministers of the gospel; one applies it to every faithful Christian, and in a special way to ministers.

cites.quote: Endure hardness - He considers a Christian minister under the notion of a soldier, not so much for his continual conflicts with the world, the devil, and the flesh, for these are in a certain sense common to all Christians, but for the hardships and difficulties to which he must be exposed who faithfully preaches the Gospel of Christ.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Having alluded to the soldier, and stated one thing in which the Christian minister is to resemble him, another point of resemblance is suggested to the mind of the apostle. Neither the minister nor the soldier is to be encumbered with the affairs of this life, and the one should not be more than the other. ... The grand purpose of the minister of the gospel is to please Christ.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The first picture is suggested by the last simile (in 2Ti 2:3 ). ... So should it be with the earnest and faithful Christian; paramount and above any earthly considerations ever must rank his Master’s service, his Master’s commands. The soldier of Christ should never allow himself to be entangled in any earthly business which would interfere with his duty to his own General.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: Consider the force of the illustrations I have given from the soldier, the contender in the games, and the husbandmen, as applying to thyself in thy ministry. ... Not intellectual perception, but personal appropriation of the truths metaphorically expressed, was what he needed to be given him by the Lord.

notes.short: An athlete is crowned only if he keeps the rules
notes.about: Paul adds a second picture: a competitor in the games is crowned only if he competes by the rules. He does not spell out the meaning: Christ's servant must serve in the way his Lord has laid down, with discipline and faithfulness, to be crowned. Paul draws on the games in 1 Corinthians 9:24-27 too.

figure.name: Hypocatastasis
figure.words: a competitor does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules
figure.means: Christ's servant, who wins the crown of reward only by serving in the way his Lord has laid down, with discipline and faithfulness

original.note: In Paul's Greek the verb for competing, athleō, is the word for contending in the public games.

notes.evidence: Barnes calls it a favorite illustration of Paul from the Grecian games, setting the minister in a contest for a crown won only by keeping its laws. Spence (Ellicott) says an athlete is chosen to stand for the servant of Christ; Clarke, that no one may look for the Lord's praise without true labor in His word; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), that Timothy is to apply it to his ministry.

cites.quote: And if a man also strive for masteries - As in the Grecian games. See this favorite illustration of Paul explained in the notes at Co1 9:24 ff. ... So the apostle here represents the Christian minister as engaged in a struggle or conflict for the crown. He says that he could not hope to win it unless he should comply with all the laws by which it is conferred

cites.quote: More accurately translated, again, if a man strive in the games. Another picture is drawn, and the picture is, as before, a well-known one to all the dwellers in the great cities of the empire. An athlete is chosen to represent the professed servant of Christ, one of those who, after long and careful training, contends in the public games

notes.short: The hardworking farmer eats first of the crop
notes.about: A third picture follows: the hardworking farmer should be the first to partake of the crops. Paul does not spell out the meaning: as the farmer's harvest comes from patient toil, so Christ's servant is to labor on, looking ahead to his reward. Then he tells Timothy to consider what he is saying.

figure.name: Hypocatastasis
figure.words: The hardworking farmer should be the first to partake of the crops
figure.means: Christ's servant, whose patient labor comes before the harvest of his reward, as a farmer must toil before he eats of his crop

notes.evidence: Spence (Ellicott) says the picture is again drawn from everyday life: patient toil wins the reward, as in the world so in religion. Clarke says the farmer must till before he reaps, and so the minister must labor before the crown. Barnes calls it an image reminding Timothy that labor comes before reward; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), an illustration Timothy is to apply to his ministry.
notes.limit: Two of the writers take the word first to mean that the farmer must toil first and eat after, rather than that he eats before anyone else.

cites.quote: Again the picture is painted from every-day life. ... It is the enduring, patient, self-sacrificing toil that is rewarded in the affairs of common life — the man that “endures hardness,” whether as a soldier, or athlete, or tiller of the ground, wins the reward; and as in the world, so in religion.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: The husbandman must first till his ground before he can expect a crop ... so the Christian minister must labor in the spiritual vineyard, and labor too under the eye and according to the direction of his Master, before he can expect that crown of righteousness that fadeth not away.

Thus understood, this would be an encouragement to Timothy to persevere in his toils, looking onward to the reward.

notes.short: Vessels of gold and of clay in a large house
notes.about: Paul pictures the church as a large house with vessels of gold and silver and also of wood and clay, some for honorable use and others for common use. Then he applies it: whoever cleanses himself of what is unfit will be a vessel for honor, useful to the Master.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: A large house contains not only vessels of gold and silver
figure.means: the church, which holds members of differing worth and use, among whom each is to keep himself clean, to be fit for the Master's service

notes.evidence: Barnes says Paul keeps up the comparison of the church with a building, its members no more alike than a house's vessels. Bullinger supplies the comparison left unsaid: so in the church are saints and reprobate. Spence (Ellicott) says the vessels stand for genuine and false members; Clarke, teachers and members. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the house is the visible church.
notes.limit: The writers differ on the vessels for common use: one sees in verse 20 members of lesser gifts and humbler work; others see false teachers and unworthy members, from whom each must keep himself clean.

cites.quote: But in a great house - Still keeping up the comparison of the church with a building. ... The application here seems to be, that in the church it is to be presumed that there will be a great variety of gifts and attainments, and that we are no more to expect that all will be alike, than we are that all the vessels in a large house will be made of gold.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.at: When the Comparison is wanting, p. 55
cites.quote: so in the great house of the church there are not only the elect saints, which are the vessels of honour, but there are the impious and reprobate, who are the vessels of dishonour

cites.quote: In a great house, argues St. Paul — still thinking of the Church, but changing the foundation image for that of a great house — are always found two distinct kinds of vessels ... By these vessels the genuine and spurious members of the Church are represented as forming two distinct classes
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: Here the apostle carries on the allusion introduced in the preceding verse. As the foundation of God refers to God's building, i.e. the whole system of Christianity, so here the great house is to be understood of the same; and the different kinds of vessels mean the different teachers, as well as the different kinds of members.
